reminder: The general linear group $GL_n(K)$ holds all invertible $n\times n$ matrices over $K$, with matrix multiplication as product.
definition: For a [field](c:field) (or commutative [ring](c:ring)) $K$, $GL_n(K)$ is the set of $n\times n$ [matrices](c:matrix) over $K$ that have an inverse matrix, with matrix multiplication as product. A matrix is invertible exactly when its [determinant](c:determinant) is a unit of $K$, so these matrices form a [group](c:group).
examples: $GL_1(K)=K^\times$, the non-zero elements of $K$ under multiplication.
$GL_2(\mathbb{R})$ holds every real $2\times 2$ matrix with non-zero determinant, such as a rotation matrix or $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
Non-example: the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $0$, so it is not in $GL_2(\mathbb{R})$.

steps: Take the [vector space](c:vector-space) $K^n$ over the field $K$.
An automorphism of $K^n$ is an invertible linear map $K^n\to K^n$.
In the standard basis, such a map is an invertible $n\times n$ matrix.
So $GL_n(K)$ is the [automorphism group](c:automorphism-group) of $K^n$ as a vector space.
links.why: Shows that $GL_n(K)$ is the symmetry group of a vector space, so the general theory of automorphism groups applies to it.

reminder: A generalized arithmetic progression is a set of integers $a+x_1d_1+\dots+x_rd_r$ in which each $x_i$ runs through a fixed finite range.
definition: A generalized arithmetic progression of rank $r$ is a set $P=\{a+x_1d_1+\dots+x_rd_r : 0\le x_i<L_i\}$ with $a$ and $d_i$ in an [abelian group](c:abelian-group), usually the [integers](c:integer), and with lengths $L_i\ge 1$. The progression is proper when all these sums are different, so that $|P|=L_1\cdots L_r$; the case $r=1$ gives an [arithmetic progression](c:arithmetic-progression).
examples: $\{x_1+100x_2 : 0\le x_1<10,\ 0\le x_2<5\}$ is a proper generalized progression of rank $2$ with $50$ elements.
Every arithmetic progression $\{a,a+d,\dots,a+(L-1)d\}$ is a generalized progression of rank $1$.
Non-example: for large $n$, the set $\{1,2,4,\dots,2^{n-1}\}$ lies in no generalized progression of bounded rank and size $O(n)$, because its sumset has about $n^2/2$ elements.

steps: Start with an [arithmetic progression](c:arithmetic-progression) $\{a,a+d,\dots,a+(L-1)d\}$.
Write it as $\{a+x_1d_1 : 0\le x_1<L_1\}$ with $d_1=d$ and $L_1=L$.
This set is a generalized arithmetic progression of rank $1$.
More steps $d_2,\dots,d_r$ then give the higher ranks.
links.why: Shows that rank $1$ is the classical case, and that higher ranks add independent step sizes.

reminder: A Riemannian manifold is geodesically complete when every geodesic extends to a geodesic defined on all of $\mathbb{R}$.
definition: A [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) (or [pseudo-Riemannian manifold](c:pseudo-riemannian-manifold)) $(X,g)$ is geodesically complete if every [geodesic](c:geodesic) extends to a geodesic defined on all of $\mathbb{R}$. Equivalently, the [exponential map](c:exponential-map) $\exp_x$ is defined on the whole tangent space $T_xX$ at every point $x$.
examples: Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is complete: its geodesics are straight lines, defined for all time.
Every compact Riemannian manifold is complete, for example the sphere $S^n$ and a flat torus.
Non-example: the plane with the origin removed is not complete, because a straight line that aims at the origin stops after a finite time.

reminder: A geodesic triangle consists of three points and three geodesic segments, one joining each pair of the points.
definition: A geodesic triangle in a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) $M$ consists of three points $p,q,r$ and three [geodesic](c:geodesic) segments that join $p$ to $q$, $q$ to $r$ and $r$ to $p$. In comparison geometry, as in Toponogov's theorem, each segment must also be a shortest path between its ends.
examples: In $\mathbb{R}^2$ the geodesics are straight lines, so the geodesic triangles are the ordinary triangles.
On the unit sphere, the octant with vertices $e_1,e_2,e_3$ is a geodesic triangle with three right angles, and its sides are great-circle arcs.
Non-example: on the sphere, three points joined by arcs of small circles do not form a geodesic triangle, because those arcs are not geodesics.

steps: Take the Euclidean plane as the [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold).
Its geodesics are the straight line segments.
Three points joined by such segments form an ordinary [triangle](c:triangle).
So an ordinary triangle is a geodesic triangle in flat space.
links.why: Shows that comparison theorems for geodesic triangles extend facts about plane triangles to curved spaces.

reminder: Geometric quantization builds a Hilbert space of quantum states from polarized sections of a prequantum line bundle on a symplectic manifold.
definition: Geometric quantization is a [quantization](c:quantization) method. It starts with a [symplectic manifold](c:symplectic-manifold) $(X,\omega)$ and a [prequantum line bundle](c:prequantum-line-bundle) whose connection has curvature $\omega$ up to a constant factor. A [polarization](c:polarization) then selects the sections that depend on half of the variables, and these sections (with a half-form correction) form a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) on which suitable classical observables act as operators.
examples: For $X=T^*\mathbb{R}^n$ with the vertical polarization, the Hilbert space is $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ of Schrödinger quantum mechanics.
A coadjoint orbit of a compact Lie group with a Kähler polarization gives an irreducible representation, as in the Borel-Weil theorem.
Non-example: prequantization alone uses all sections of the line bundle, which gives a space that is too large, so a polarization is also needed.

steps: A classical system is a [symplectic manifold](c:symplectic-manifold) of states with observables as functions.
[Quantization](c:quantization) asks for a Hilbert space and operators for these observables.
Geometric quantization takes sections of a prequantum line bundle as candidate states.
A polarization cuts these sections down to the Hilbert space.
links.why: Shows geometric quantization as one concrete recipe for the general task of quantization.

reminder: The P representation writes a quantum state of light as a mixture of coherent states with a quasi-probability weight $P(\alpha)$.
definition: The Glauber-Sudarshan P representation of a [density operator](c:density-operator) $\rho$ of one field mode is a function or [distribution](c:distribution) $P$ on the [complex plane](c:complex-number) with $\rho=\int P(\alpha)\,|\alpha\rangle\langle\alpha|\,d^2\alpha$, where the $|\alpha\rangle$ are [coherent states](c:coherent-state). It satisfies $\int P\,d^2\alpha=1$, but it can be negative or singular, so it is a quasi-probability distribution.
examples: A coherent state $|\beta\rangle$ has $P(\alpha)=\delta^2(\alpha-\beta)$.
A thermal state with mean photon number $\bar n>0$ has the Gaussian $P(\alpha)=\frac{1}{\pi\bar n}e^{-|\alpha|^2/\bar n}$.
Non-example: the single-photon state $|1\rangle$ has no non-negative $P$; its $P$ involves derivatives of the delta function, which marks the state as non-classical.

reminder: The global dimension of a ring is the supremum of the projective dimensions of all its modules.
definition: The (left) global dimension of a [ring](c:ring) $R$ is the supremum of $\operatorname{pd}M$ over all left [modules](c:module) $M$, where the [projective dimension](c:projective-dimension) $\operatorname{pd}M$ is the length of a shortest resolution of $M$ by [projective modules](c:projective-module). Equivalently, it is the least $n$ with $\operatorname{Ext}^{n+1}_R(M,N)=0$ for all modules $M,N$, or $\infty$ if no such $n$ exists; see [Ext groups](c:ext-group).
examples: A field has global dimension $0$, and so does every semisimple ring.
$\mathbb{Z}$ has global dimension $1$, because it is a principal ideal domain that is not a field.
The polynomial ring $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ over a field $k$ has global dimension $n$ (Hilbert's syzygy theorem).
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$ has no finite global dimension, because the module $\mathbb{Z}/2$ has no finite projective resolution.

reminder: A good open cover is an open cover in which every non-empty finite intersection of its sets is contractible.
definition: A good open cover of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is an [open cover](c:open-cover) $\{U_i\}$ such that every non-empty finite intersection $U_{i_1}\cap\dots\cap U_{i_k}$ is a [contractible space](c:contractible-space). For a manifold, one often asks instead that each such intersection is diffeomorphic to a [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space).
examples: On $\mathbb{R}^n$, every cover by open balls is good, because each finite intersection of balls is convex and so contractible.
Three open arcs of $160^\circ$ with centres $120^\circ$ apart cover $S^1$, and each non-empty finite intersection is an arc, so this cover is good.
Non-example: two open arcs that cover $S^1$ meet in two disjoint arcs, which is not contractible.

steps: Take any [open cover](c:open-cover) $\{U_i\}$ of a space $X$.
Look at every non-empty finite intersection of its sets.
Add the condition that each such intersection is contractible.
An open cover with this extra condition is a good open cover.
links.why: Shows that a good cover is an ordinary cover with one extra condition, the condition that makes Čech methods and the nerve theorem work.

reminder: A graded algebra splits as a direct sum of pieces labelled by a monoid, and products add the labels: $A_mA_n\subseteq A_{m+n}$.
definition: A graded algebra over a [ring](c:ring) $R$ is an [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) $A$ with a [monoid](c:monoid) $M$ (often $\mathbb{N}$ or $\mathbb{Z}$) and a [direct sum](c:direct-sum) decomposition $A=\bigoplus_{m\in M}A_m$ of $R$-modules such that $A_mA_n\subseteq A_{m+n}$ for all $m,n$. Elements of $A_m$ are homogeneous of degree $m$.
examples: The polynomial ring $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ is graded by $\mathbb{N}$, and $A_d$ is the space of homogeneous polynomials of degree $d$.
The tensor algebra $T(V)=\bigoplus_{d\ge0}V^{\otimes d}$ of a vector space $V$ is graded by $\mathbb{N}$.
Non-example: $k[x]/(x^2-1)$ has no $\mathbb{N}$-grading with $\deg x=1$, because the relation $x^2=1$ would put $1$ in degrees $2$ and $0$; it is graded by $\mathbb{Z}/2$ instead.

steps: Take an [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) $A$ over a ring $R$.
Choose a monoid $M$ and split $A$ into a direct sum of pieces $A_m$ with $m\in M$.
Require that $A_mA_n\subseteq A_{m+n}$ for all $m,n\in M$.
An algebra with such a splitting is a graded algebra.
links.why: Shows that a graded algebra is an ordinary algebra plus a degree bookkeeping that products respect.

reminder: A graded module over a graded ring is a direct sum of pieces $M_n$ with $R_mM_n\subseteq M_{m+n}$.
definition: Let $R=\bigoplus_mR_m$ be a [graded ring](c:graded-ring). A graded $R$-[module](c:module) is a module $M$ with a [direct sum](c:direct-sum) decomposition $M=\bigoplus_nM_n$ into additive subgroups such that $R_mM_n\subseteq M_{m+n}$ for all $m,n$. Elements of $M_n$ are homogeneous of degree $n$.
examples: The ring $R=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ is a graded module over itself, and so is every homogeneous ideal and every quotient $R/I$ by one.
A free $R$-module with basis elements placed in chosen degrees $a_1,\dots,a_r$ is a graded module.
Non-example: $k[x]/(x-1)$ has no grading as a $k[x]$-module, because $x$ acts as the identity, so a non-zero homogeneous $m$ would satisfy $m=xm$ in two different degrees.

steps: Take a [module](c:module) $M$ over a graded ring $R$.
Split $M$ as a direct sum of subgroups $M_n$.
Require $R_mM_n\subseteq M_{m+n}$, so that multiplication respects degrees.
A module with such a splitting is a graded module.
links.why: Shows that a graded module is a module with a degree splitting that the ring action respects.

reminder: The closure of a graph repeatedly joins two non-adjacent vertices whose degrees add up to at least the number of vertices.
definition: For a [graph](c:graph) $G$ with $n$ [vertices](c:vertex), the closure $\operatorname{cl}(G)$ is the graph that results when you repeatedly add an [edge](c:edge) $uv$ between non-adjacent vertices whose [degrees](c:vertex-degree) in the current graph satisfy $\deg u+\deg v\ge n$, until no such pair remains. The result does not depend on the order of the additions. This threshold $n$ serves Hamiltonian cycles, and a lower threshold such as $n-1$ serves Hamiltonian paths.
examples: If every vertex has degree at least $n/2$, then $\operatorname{cl}(G)=K_n$, because any two non-adjacent vertices have degree sum at least $n$.
The cycle $C_n$ with $n\ge5$ is its own closure, because any two vertices have degree sum $4<n$.
Non-example: adding an edge between two non-adjacent vertices with $\deg u+\deg v<n$ is not a closure step.

reminder: A greedy algorithm builds a solution step by step and always takes the best local choice without undoing it.
definition: A greedy [algorithm](c:algorithm) builds its answer in steps. At each step it takes the option that looks best by a fixed local rule, and it never changes an earlier choice. For some problems the final answer is always correct, and for other problems it is only an approximation.
examples: Zeckendorf representation: subtract the largest Fibonacci number not above $n$, then repeat with the remainder.
Kruskal's algorithm for a minimum spanning tree adds the cheapest edge that creates no cycle.
Coin change with coins $1,3,4$ and amount $6$: the greedy rule takes $4+1+1$, which is three coins although $3+3$ uses two, so greedy is not optimal here.
Non-example: exhaustive backtracking search is not greedy, because it returns to earlier choices and tries other options.

reminder: A Grothendieck site is a category with a Grothendieck topology, which says which families of morphisms into each object count as covers.
definition: A Grothendieck site is a [category](c:category) $C$ with a Grothendieck topology $J$: for each object $U$, a set $J(U)$ of [covering sieves](c:covering-sieve) on $U$. These satisfy three rules: the maximal sieve covers, the [pullback](c:pullback) of a covering sieve along any morphism covers, and a sieve that covers locally on a covering sieve is itself covering.
examples: For a topological space $X$, the category of open sets with the usual open covers is a site.
The category of schemes with the étale topology is a site, where covers are jointly surjective families of étale maps.
Non-example: a category with $J(U)=\emptyset$ for every $U$ is no site, because the maximal sieve must be a cover.

steps: Take a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ and its open sets as a category with inclusions as morphisms.
Call a family of inclusions $V_i\subseteq U$ a cover when $\bigcup_iV_i=U$.
These covers satisfy the three rules of a Grothendieck topology.
So every topological space gives a site, and a general site allows other kinds of covers.
links.why: Shows that sites are the setting for sheaf theory beyond topological spaces, with the same pattern of covers.

reminder: The group algebra $R[G]$ has the elements of $G$ as a basis and multiplies basis elements as the group does.
definition: For a [group](c:group) $G$ and a commutative [ring](c:ring) $R$, the group algebra $R[G]$ is the [free module](c:free-module) on the set $G$, with elements $\sum_ga_gg$ (finite sums with $a_g\in R$). Its product is $\left(\sum_ga_gg\right)\left(\sum_hb_hh\right)=\sum_{g,h}a_gb_h\,gh$, which makes $R[G]$ an [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) over $R$.
examples: For the cyclic group $C_2=\{1,g\}$, $\mathbb{Q}[C_2]\cong\mathbb{Q}\times\mathbb{Q}$ by $g\mapsto(1,-1)$.
$\mathbb{C}[\mathbb{Z}]$ is the ring $\mathbb{C}[t,t^{-1}]$ of Laurent polynomials.
Non-example: the algebra $R^G$ of functions $G\to R$ with pointwise product is commutative even when $G$ is not, so it is not $R[G]$, whose product is a convolution.

steps: Take the [free module](c:free-module) $R[G]$ with basis the set $G$.
Extend the product of $G$ bilinearly to all finite sums.
Associativity of $G$ gives associativity of the extended product.
The identity element of $G$ is the unit, so $R[G]$ is an associative algebra.
links.why: Shows that general algebra theory applies to $R[G]$, and that its structure reflects the group.

reminder: The group determinant of a finite group is the determinant of the matrix $(x_{gh^{-1}})$ with one variable for each group element.
definition: For a [finite group](c:finite-group) $G$, give each element $g$ a variable $x_g$. The group determinant is the [determinant](c:determinant) of the $|G|\times|G|$ [matrix](c:matrix) with $(g,h)$ entry $x_{gh^{-1}}$, which is a homogeneous [polynomial](c:polynomial) of degree $|G|$ in the variables $x_g$.
examples: For $G=\mathbb{Z}/2$, the group determinant is $x_0^2-x_1^2=(x_0-x_1)(x_0+x_1)$.
For $G=\mathbb{Z}/3$, it is the circulant determinant $x_0^3+x_1^3+x_2^3-3x_0x_1x_2$, a product of three linear factors.
Non-example: the determinant of one fixed matrix $\rho(g)$ from a representation is a number, not a polynomial in $|G|$ variables.

reminder: A group of Lie type is the group $G(k)$ of $k$-rational points of a reductive linear algebraic group $G$.
definition: A group of Lie type over a [field](c:field) $k$ is the group $G(k)$ of [rational points](c:rational-point) with values in $k$ of a [reductive group](c:reductive-group) $G$, which is a linear [algebraic group](c:algebraic-group). When $k$ is a finite field, $G(k)$ is a [finite group](c:finite-group).
examples: $GL_n(\mathbb{F}_q)$ and $SL_n(\mathbb{F}_q)$ are finite groups of Lie type, from the reductive groups $GL_n$ and $SL_n$.
$SL_2(\mathbb{R})$ and $Sp_{2n}(\mathbb{C})$ are groups of Lie type over $\mathbb{R}$ and over $\mathbb{C}$.
Non-example: the Monster group is a finite simple group that is not of Lie type.

reminder: A group representation is a homomorphism from a group $G$ to the group of invertible linear maps of a vector space $V$.
definition: A representation of a [group](c:group) $G$ on a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ is a [group homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism) $\rho:G\to GL(V)$ into the [general linear group](c:general-linear-group) of $V$. Equivalently, each $g$ acts as an invertible linear map $\rho(g)$ with $\rho(gh)=\rho(g)\rho(h)$ and $\rho(1)=\mathrm{id}_V$.
examples: The permutation representation of $S_n$ on $\mathbb{C}^n$ permutes the coordinates.
The map $\mathbb{Z}\to GL_1(\mathbb{C})$, $n\mapsto e^{in\theta}$, is a one-dimensional representation of $\mathbb{Z}$.
Non-example: the map $S_3\to GL_1(\mathbb{C})$ that sends every transposition $t$ to $2$ is not a homomorphism, because $\rho(t)^2=4$ but $t^2=1$.

steps: Take a [group action](c:group-action) of $G$ on a set $X$.
Let $X$ be a vector space $V$.
Require that every $g$ acts as a linear map $V\to V$.
Such an action is the same as a homomorphism $G\to GL(V)$, that is, a representation.
links.why: Shows that a representation is a group action by linear maps, so facts about actions apply to it.

reminder: The order of growth of an entire function $f$ is the number $\rho$ such that its maximum modulus grows like $\exp(r^{\rho})$.
definition: For an [entire function](c:entire-function) $f$, put $M(r)=\max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|$. The order of $f$ is $\rho=\limsup_{r\to\infty}\frac{\log\log M(r)}{\log r}$, using the [limit superior](c:limit-superior) and the [logarithm](c:logarithm). The same formula, with the maximum taken over the part of each circle inside the domain, defines the order of a holomorphic function on an unbounded domain such as a sector.
examples: Polynomials have order $0$.
$e^z$ and $\sin z$ have order $1$, and $e^{z^2}$ has order $2$.
Non-example: $e^{e^z}$ has no finite order, because $\log\log M(r)=r$ grows faster than $\log r$.

reminder: The Hadamard gate is the one-qubit gate with matrix $\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$, which turns each basis state into an equal superposition.
definition: The Hadamard gate $H$ is the [quantum logic gate](c:quantum-logic-gate) on one [qubit](c:qbit) with [matrix](c:matrix) $H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$. It maps $|0\rangle$ to $(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and $|1\rangle$ to $(|0\rangle-|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$, and as a [linear map](c:linear-map) it is unitary with $H^2=1$.
examples: $H|0\rangle=|+\rangle$ and $H|1\rangle=|-\rangle$, the two equal superpositions.
Applying $H$ twice gives back the original state, because $H^2=1$.
Non-example: the Pauli $X$ gate sends $|0\rangle$ to $|1\rangle$; it is a different one-qubit gate and makes no superposition.

steps: A one-qubit [quantum logic gate](c:quantum-logic-gate) is a $2\times2$ unitary matrix.
The columns of $H$ are orthonormal, so $H$ is unitary.
Hence $H$ is a one-qubit gate, the one that sends each basis state to an equal superposition.
links.why: Shows that the Hadamard gate is one particular unitary among all one-qubit gates.

reminder: A half-plane is the part of the plane on one side of a straight line.
definition: A half-plane is a set $\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2 : ax+by>c\}$ with [real numbers](c:real-number) $a,b,c$ and $(a,b)\ne(0,0)$, that is, the points strictly on one side of the [line](c:line) $ax+by=c$. A closed half-plane uses $\ge$ and also contains the line.
examples: The upper half-plane $\{z\in\mathbb{C} : \operatorname{Im}z>0\}$.
The right half-plane $\{z\in\mathbb{C} : \operatorname{Re}z>0\}$, where Laplace transforms of many functions converge.
Non-example: the strip $\{z : 0<\operatorname{Im}z<1\}$ lies between two lines, so it is not a half-plane.

steps: Take the real axis, the line $\operatorname{Im}z=0$.
Take the points strictly above it, which satisfy $\operatorname{Im}z>0$.
This set is the [upper half plane](c:upper-half-plane).
So the upper half plane is the half-plane for one chosen line and side.
links.why: Shows that results proved for the upper half plane carry over to every half-plane by a rotation and a shift.

reminder: A Hamiltonian action of a Lie group on a symplectic manifold acts by symplectomorphisms, and each generator is a Hamiltonian vector field.
definition: An action of a [Lie group](c:lie-group) $G$ on a [symplectic manifold](c:symplectic-manifold) $(X,\omega)$ is Hamiltonian if every $g$ acts as a [symplectomorphism](c:symplectomorphism) and every element $\xi$ of the [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) generates the [Hamiltonian vector field](c:hamiltonian-vector-field) of a function $H_\xi$ on $X$. The functions $H_\xi$ must depend linearly and equivariantly on $\xi$, and together they give the momentum map.
examples: The rotation of the sphere $S^2$ about the vertical axis, with the area form, is Hamiltonian, and its generator is the Hamiltonian vector field of the height function $z$.
The translation action of $\mathbb{R}^n$ on $T^*\mathbb{R}^n$ is Hamiltonian, with the momentum components $p_i$ as the functions $H_\xi$.
Non-example: translation of the torus $T^2$ in one direction keeps the area form but is not Hamiltonian, because $\iota_\xi\omega$ is closed and not exact.

steps: Take a smooth [action](c:lie-group-action) of a Lie group $G$ on a manifold $X$.
Give $X$ a symplectic form $\omega$ and ask that $G$ preserves $\omega$.
Ask also that every generator of the action is a Hamiltonian vector field.
An action with these conditions is a Hamiltonian action.
links.why: Shows that a Hamiltonian action is a symplectic action whose generators have Hamiltonian functions, which gives the momentum map.

reminder: A harmonic map between Riemannian manifolds is a critical point of the Dirichlet energy, so its tension field is zero.
definition: A [smooth map](c:smooth-map) $f:(M,g)\to(N,h)$ between [Riemannian manifolds](c:riemannian-manifold) is harmonic if it is a [critical point](c:critical-point) of the energy [functional](c:functional) $E(f)=\frac12\int_M|df|^2\,d\mathrm{vol}_g$ for variations with compact support. Equivalently, its tension field $\tau(f)=\operatorname{tr}\nabla df$ is zero.
examples: A function $f:M\to\mathbb{R}$ is a harmonic map exactly when $\Delta f=0$.
A geodesic with constant speed, seen as a map from an interval, is a harmonic map.
Non-example: $f(x)=x^2$ from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}$ is not harmonic, because $f''=2\ne0$.

steps: Take a [harmonic function](c:harmonic-function) $u:M\to\mathbb{R}$ on a Riemannian manifold $M$.
View $u$ as a map into the target $\mathbb{R}$ with its standard metric.
For this target, the tension field of $u$ is the Laplacian $\Delta u$.
So $u$ is harmonic as a function exactly when it is a harmonic map.
links.why: Shows that harmonic maps extend the Laplace equation from real-valued functions to maps into curved targets.

steps: Take a curve $\gamma:I\to N$ from an interval $I$ with its standard metric.
For this domain, the tension field of $\gamma$ is the covariant acceleration $\nabla_{\gamma'}\gamma'$.
It is zero exactly when $\gamma$ is a [geodesic](c:geodesic) with constant speed.
So the constant-speed geodesics are the harmonic maps from intervals.
links.why: Shows that harmonic maps extend geodesics from one-dimensional domains to domains of any dimension.

reminder: A metric space has the Besicovitch covering property if, for some $N$ and $\tau>1$, it has no satellite configuration of $N+1$ points.
definition: A [metric space](c:metric-space) has the Besicovitch covering property if there are $N$ and $\tau>1$ such that no satellite configuration of parameter $\tau$ with $N+1$ points exists. Such a configuration is a family of $N+1$ [balls](c:ball) such that the last ball meets all the others, and any two balls are ordered: the centre of the later ball is not inside the earlier ball, and the later radius is at most $\tau$ times the earlier radius.
examples: Every finite-dimensional real normed space, such as $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the Euclidean metric, has the property; this gives the Besicovitch covering theorem.
A finite metric space with $m$ points has the property with $N=m$, because the centres of a satellite configuration are different points.

Non-example: in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, the origin and unit vectors $e_1,\dots,e_N$, each with a ball of radius $1$, form a satellite configuration for every $N$, so the property fails.

reminder: A random variable $X$ is sub-Gaussian with parameter $c$ if $\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]\le e^{ct^2/2}$ for every real $t$.
definition: A real [random variable](c:random-variable) $X$ has a sub-Gaussian [moment-generating function](c:moment-generating-function) with parameter $c\ge0$ if $e^{tX}$ is [integrable](c:integrable-function) for every real $t$ and $\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]\le e^{ct^2/2}$ for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$. This bound forces $\mathbb{E}[X]=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}X\le c$.
examples: A normal variable $N(0,\sigma^2)$ is sub-Gaussian with $c=\sigma^2$.
A Rademacher variable, equal to $\pm1$ with probability $\tfrac12$ each, is sub-Gaussian with $c=1$, because $\cosh t\le e^{t^2/2}$.
A centred variable with values in $[a,b]$ is sub-Gaussian with $c=(b-a)^2/4$ (Hoeffding's lemma).
Non-example: the centred exponential variable $Y=E-1$ with $E\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ has an infinite moment-generating function for $t\ge1$, so it is not sub-Gaussian.

steps: Take a variable $X\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ with a [normal distribution](c:normal-distribution).
Its moment-generating function is $\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]=e^{\sigma^2t^2/2}$ for every real $t$.
So the sub-Gaussian bound holds with $c=\sigma^2$, even with equality.
Hence every centred normal variable is sub-Gaussian.
links.why: Shows that sub-Gaussian variables keep the Gaussian tail bound while allowing many other distributions.

reminder: Hereditary base-$b$ notation writes a number in base $b$, then writes every large exponent in base $b$ again, and so on.
definition: Take the [base expansion](c:base-p-expansion) of a [natural number](c:natural-number) $n$ in base $b\ge2$, that is, $n=\sum_ic_ib^{e_i}$ with $0<c_i<b$. Then write each exponent $e_i\ge b$ in base $b$ in the same way, and repeat until every exponent is smaller than $b$.
examples: Non-example: the ordinary base-$2$ expansion $100=2^6+2^5+2^2$ is not hereditary, because the exponents $6,5,2$ are at least $2$ and are not yet expanded.

reminder: A Hermitian-Einstein metric on a holomorphic vector bundle has constant mean curvature: $i\Lambda F_h=\lambda\,\mathrm{id}$.
definition: Let $E$ be a [holomorphic vector bundle](c:holomorphic-vector-bundle) over a [Kähler manifold](c:kahler-manifold) $(X,\omega)$. A Hermitian metric $h$ on $E$ is Hermitian-Einstein if the [curvature](c:curvature) $F_h$ of its [Chern connection](c:chern-connection) satisfies $i\Lambda_\omega F_h=\lambda\,\mathrm{id}_E$ for a constant $\lambda$, where $\Lambda_\omega$ is the contraction with $\omega$.
examples: A flat unitary metric has $F_h=0$, so it is Hermitian-Einstein with $\lambda=0$.
On a Kähler-Einstein manifold, the metric that the Kähler metric induces on the holomorphic tangent bundle is Hermitian-Einstein.
Non-example: the bundle $\mathcal{O}\oplus\mathcal{O}(1)$ on $\mathbb{CP}^1$ has no Hermitian-Einstein metric, because it is not polystable (Donaldson-Uhlenbeck-Yau).

steps: Take a [Kähler manifold](c:kahler-manifold) $(X,\omega)$ and its holomorphic tangent bundle $T_X$.
The Kähler metric induces a Hermitian metric $h$ on $T_X$.
The mean curvature $i\Lambda F_h$ of $h$ is the Ricci curvature of $\omega$, seen as an endomorphism of $T_X$.
So $h$ is Hermitian-Einstein exactly when $\omega$ is [Kähler-Einstein](c:kahler-einstein-manifold).
links.why: Shows that the Hermitian-Einstein condition extends the Kähler-Einstein condition from the tangent bundle to any holomorphic bundle.

reminder: The Hilbert transform $Hf$ is the principal-value convolution of $f$ with $1/(\pi x)$.
definition: The Hilbert transform of a function $f$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is $Hf(x)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{p.v.}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{f(y)}{x-y}\,dy$, the [convolution](c:convolution) of $f$ with $1/(\pi x)$ taken as a [Cauchy principal value](c:cauchy-principal-value). On the [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) side, it multiplies $\hat f(\xi)$ by $-i\,\operatorname{sgn}(\xi)$.
examples: $H(\cos)=\sin$ and $H(\sin)=-\cos$.
The Hilbert transform of the indicator function of $[0,1]$ is $\frac1\pi\log\left|\frac{x}{x-1}\right|$.
Non-example: the ordinary integral of $f(y)/(x-y)$ diverges when $f$ is continuous and $f(x)\ne0$, because $1/x$ is not locally integrable; only the principal value works.

reminder: The Hochschild cohomology $HH^n(A,M)$ of an algebra $A$ with coefficients in a bimodule $M$ is $\operatorname{Ext}^n_{A\otimes A^{op}}(A,M)$.
definition: For an [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) $A$ over a field $k$ and an $A$-[bimodule](c:bimodule) $M$, the Hochschild cohomology $HH^n(A,M)$ is the cohomology of the [cochain complex](c:cochain-complex) $C^n(A,M)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(A^{\otimes n},M)$ with the Hochschild differential. Equivalently, $HH^n(A,M)$ is an [Ext group](c:ext-group), $\operatorname{Ext}^n_{A\otimes A^{op}}(A,M)$, and $HH^*(A)$ means $HH^*(A,A)$.
examples: $HH^0(A,A)$ is the centre of $A$, and $HH^1(A,A)$ is the space of derivations modulo inner derivations.
For $A=k[x]$, $HH^n(A,A)=0$ for all $n\ge2$.
For a smooth commutative algebra over a field of characteristic $0$, $HH^*(A,A)$ is the algebra of polyvector fields (the Hochschild-Kostant-Rosenberg theorem).
Non-example: Hochschild homology $HH_n(A)$ uses the tensor product over $A\otimes A^{op}$ instead of $\operatorname{Hom}$; it is the dual theory, not Hochschild cohomology.

steps: Bimodules over $A$ are the same as modules over $A^e=A\otimes A^{op}$.
Regard $A$ itself as an $A^e$-module.
Form the [Ext group](c:ext-group) $\operatorname{Ext}^n_{A^e}(A,M)$ for a bimodule $M$.
These Ext groups are the Hochschild cohomology groups $HH^n(A,M)$.
links.why: Shows that Hochschild cohomology is a particular Ext group, so tools of homological algebra compute it.

reminder: A holomorphic matrix function is a matrix-valued function on an open set of $\mathbb{C}$ whose entries are all holomorphic.
definition: A holomorphic matrix function on an [open set](c:open-set) $U\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ is a map $F:U\to\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$ into the space of [matrices](c:matrix) whose entries $F_{ij}$ are all [holomorphic functions](c:holomorphic-function). Equivalently, $F$ is complex differentiable as a map into this space.
examples: $F(z)=\begin{pmatrix}1&z\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb{C}$.
$F(z)=e^{zA}=\sum_{k\ge0}z^kA^k/k!$ for a fixed matrix $A$ is an entire matrix function.
Non-example: $F(z)=\begin{pmatrix}\bar z&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has the entry $\bar z$, which is not holomorphic.

steps: Take a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) $f:U\to\mathbb{C}$.
Identify $f$ with the $1\times1$ matrix $(f(z))$.
Its only entry is holomorphic, so it is a holomorphic matrix function.
links.why: Shows that matrix functions extend scalar holomorphic functions, and that size $n=1$ is the classical case.

reminder: A section of a jet bundle is holonomic when it is the jet $j^rf$ of an actual section $f$.
definition: Let $E\to X$ be a fiber bundle and $J^rE$ its [jet bundle](c:jet-bundle). A [section](c:section) $F$ of $J^rE\to X$ is holonomic if $F=j^rf$ for some section $f$ of $E$, that is, if its jet components are the actual derivatives of its base component $f$. Other sections of $J^rE$ are called formal.
examples: For $f(x)=x^2$, the section $x\mapsto(x,x^2,2x)$ of $J^1(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$ equals $j^1f$, so it is holonomic.
Every jet prolongation $j^rf$ of a smooth section $f$ is holonomic by definition.
Non-example: the section $x\mapsto(x,0,1)$ of $J^1(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$ would need $f=0$ and $f'=1$ at once, so it is formal and not holonomic.

steps: Take a [section](c:section) $F=(f,f_1,\dots,f_r)$ of the jet bundle $J^rE\to X$.
Here $f$ is the base component and $f_k$ are the jet components.
Ask that each $f_k$ equals the $k$-th derivative of $f$.
A section with this condition is $j^rf$, a holonomic section.
links.why: Shows that holonomic sections are exactly the sections of the jet bundle that come from honest sections of $E$.

reminder: The holonomy of a connection around a loop is the automorphism of the fiber given by parallel transport once around the loop.
definition: Let $\nabla$ be a [connection](c:connection-on-a-bundle) on a bundle over $X$ and let $\gamma$ be a loop in $X$ based at $x_0$. The holonomy of $\nabla$ along $\gamma$ is the [parallel transport](c:parallel-transport) around $\gamma$, an [automorphism](c:automorphism) of the [fiber](c:fiber) over $x_0$ (an element of the structure group $G$ for a principal $G$-bundle).
examples: On the unit sphere $S^2$ with the Levi-Civita connection, transport around a simple loop that encloses area $A$ rotates tangent vectors by the angle $A$.
The connection $d+ia\,d\varphi$ with constant $a$ on the trivial line bundle over the circle has holonomy $e^{-2\pi ia}$ around the circle.
Non-example: parallel transport along a path from $x_0$ to a different point $x_1$ maps one fiber to another fiber, so it is not a holonomy.

steps: Take [parallel transport](c:parallel-transport) of $\nabla$ along a path $\gamma:[0,1]\to X$.
It is an isomorphism from the fiber over $\gamma(0)$ to the fiber over $\gamma(1)$.
Choose $\gamma$ to be a loop, so that $\gamma(0)=\gamma(1)=x_0$.
Then both fibers are the same, and the transport is an automorphism of that fiber: the holonomy.
links.why: Shows that holonomy is parallel transport along closed loops, and that this is where curvature becomes visible.

reminder: The holonomy group at a point $x$ is the group of all holonomies of a connection around loops based at $x$.
definition:
Let $
abla$ be a [connection](c:connection-on-a-bundle) on a bundle over $X$ and let $x\in X$. The holonomy group $\mathrm{Hol}_x(
abla)$ is the set of [holonomies](c:holonomy) of $
abla$ along all piecewise smooth loops based at $x$, with composition as product. It is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of the [automorphism group](c:automorphism-group) of the fiber over $x$, or of the structure group $G$ for a principal $G$-bundle.
examples: For the Levi-Civita connection of the round sphere $S^2$, the holonomy group is $SO(2)$.
A flat connection on a simply connected manifold has trivial holonomy group.
The Levi-Civita connection of a flat torus has trivial holonomy group.
Non-example: the set of parallel transports along all paths that start at $x$ is no group, because transports along non-closed paths end in other fibers.

reminder: A homogeneous form of degree $d$ is a polynomial whose monomials all have total degree $d$.
definition: A homogeneous form of degree $d$ in the variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$ is a [polynomial](c:polynomial) all of whose monomials have total [degree](c:degree-of-a-polynomial) $d$. Over an infinite field, this is equivalent to $F(\lambda x)=\lambda^dF(x)$ for every scalar $\lambda$.
examples: $x^2+xy+3y^2$ is a form of degree $2$, and $x^3+y^3+z^3-3xyz$ is a form of degree $3$.
A linear form $a_1x_1+\dots+a_nx_n$ is a form of degree $1$.
Non-example: $x^2+y$ has monomials of degrees $2$ and $1$, so it is not homogeneous.

steps: Take a [polynomial](c:polynomial) $F$ in the variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$.
Group its monomials by total degree.
Require that only one total degree $d$ occurs.
A polynomial with this condition is a homogeneous form of degree $d$.
links.why: Shows that a form is a polynomial with all its terms in one degree, which is why it scales by $\lambda^d$.

steps: Take a [quadratic form](c:quadratic-form) $Q(x)=\sum a_{ij}x_ix_j$ in $n$ variables.
Every monomial $x_ix_j$ has total degree $2$.
So $Q$ is a homogeneous form of degree $2$.
Forms of other degrees $d$ extend the idea.
links.why: Shows that quadratic forms are the degree $2$ case, and that results on forms of degree $d$ include them.

reminder: A homogeneous space is a space together with a transitive action of a group $G$ on it.
definition: A homogeneous $G$-space is a space $X$, such as a [topological space](c:topological-space) or a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold), with a [group action](c:group-action) of a group $G$ of the matching kind, such as a [Lie group](c:lie-group), by structure-preserving maps, and the action is [transitive](c:transitive-action). Any two points of $X$ are then related by some $g\in G$, and $X\cong G/H$ as sets, where $H$ is the stabilizer of a point.
examples: The sphere $S^n=SO(n+1)/SO(n)$ is a homogeneous space of $SO(n+1)$.
The space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a homogeneous space of the translation group $\mathbb{R}^n$.
Non-example: $S^2$ with the group $SO(2)$ that rotates about the vertical axis is not homogeneous, because the orbits are circles of latitude and the action is not transitive.

steps: Take a [group action](c:group-action) of a group $G$ on a space $X$.
Ask that the action is transitive: for all $x,y\in X$ there is a $g$ with $gx=y$.
Then $X$ is a single orbit.
A space with such a single-orbit action is a homogeneous space.
links.why: Shows that homogeneous spaces are the group actions with one orbit, and so are all of the form $G/H$.

reminder: A homology equivalence is a map that induces isomorphisms on the homology groups in every degree.
definition: A continuous map $f:X\to Y$ of [topological spaces](c:topological-space) is a homology equivalence if the induced map $f_*:H_n(X)\to H_n(Y)$ on [homology](c:homology) is an [isomorphism](c:isomorphism) for every $n\ge0$. The same word is used for a chain map that induces isomorphisms on homology.
examples: Every homotopy equivalence is a homology equivalence.
Quillen's plus construction gives a map $X\to X^+$ that is a homology equivalence.
For a non-trivial acyclic group $G$, the map $BG\to *$ is a homology equivalence but not a homotopy equivalence.
Non-example: the inclusion of a point into the circle $S^1$ is not a homology equivalence, because $H_1(*)=0$ and $H_1(S^1)=\mathbb{Z}$.

steps: Take a [weak homotopy equivalence](c:weak-homotopy-equivalence) $f:X\to Y$.
Singular homology is invariant under weak homotopy equivalence.
So $f$ induces isomorphisms on all homology groups.
Hence every weak homotopy equivalence is a homology equivalence, but the converse can fail.
links.why: Shows that a homology equivalence is a weaker notion of sameness, which is why it can fail to be a homotopy equivalence.

reminder: A homotopy pullback is a pullback taken up to homotopy: replacing the diagram by a weakly equivalent one does not change it.
definition: For maps $f:X\to Z$ and $g:Y\to Z$ of spaces, the homotopy pullback is the space of triples $(x,y,\gamma)$ with $x\in X$, $y\in Y$ and $\gamma$ a path in $Z$ from $f(x)$ to $g(y)$. It is a [pullback](c:pullback) in which the equality $f(x)=g(y)$ is replaced by a [homotopy](c:homotopy), and it is invariant under [weak homotopy equivalence](c:weak-homotopy-equivalence) of the diagram.
examples: The homotopy fiber of $f:X\to Z$ is the homotopy pullback of $*\to Z\leftarrow X$.
The loop space $\Omega Z$ is the homotopy pullback of $*\to Z\leftarrow *$.
An ordinary pullback along a fibration is already a homotopy pullback.
Non-example: the ordinary pullback of $\{0\}\to[0,1]\leftarrow\{1\}$ is empty, but the homotopy pullback is contractible, so the ordinary pullback is not a homotopy pullback here.

steps: Take a cospan $X\to Z\leftarrow Y$ in which one map is a fibration.
Then the ordinary [pullback](c:pullback) $X\times_ZY$ is weakly equivalent to the homotopy pullback.
So ordinary pullbacks along fibrations are homotopy pullbacks.
For general maps, replace one map by a fibration first.
links.why: Shows that the homotopy pullback repairs the ordinary pullback, which is only correct when one map is a fibration.

reminder: The Honda formal group law of height $n$ at a prime $p$ has $p$-series $[p](x)=x^{p^n}$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$.
definition: For a prime $p$ and $n\ge1$, the Honda formal group law of height $n$ is the $p$-typical [formal group law](c:formal-group-law) over $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ with [logarithm](c:logarithm) $\sum_{k\ge0}x^{p^{nk}}/p^k$. Reduced modulo $p$, it has $p$-series $[p](x)=x^{p^n}$, so it has height $n$.
examples: At height $n=1$, it is isomorphic over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ to the multiplicative formal group law $x+y+xy$.
Its reduction over $\mathbb{F}_p$ is the formal group law of Morava K-theory $K(n)$.
Non-example: the additive formal group law $x+y$ has $[p](x)=0$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$, so it has no finite height and is not a Honda law.

steps: Take a [formal group law](c:formal-group-law) over a torsion-free ring such as $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$.
Such a law is determined by its logarithm over the rational numbers.
The logarithm $\sum_{k\ge0}x^{p^{nk}}/p^k$ defines a law with $p$-integral coefficients.
That law is the Honda formal group law of height $n$.
links.why: Shows that the Honda law is one explicit formal group law, chosen by its logarithm, with a prescribed height.

reminder: An equilibrium of a differential equation is hyperbolic when its linearization has no eigenvalue with real part zero.
definition: For an [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) $\dot x=f(x)$, an equilibrium $x^*$, that is, a point with $f(x^*)=0$, is hyperbolic if the [Jacobian matrix](c:jacobian-matrix) $Df(x^*)$ has no [eigenvalue](c:eigenvalue) with real part $0$. For a map, a [fixed point](c:fixed-point) is hyperbolic if the Jacobian has no eigenvalue of modulus $1$.
examples: The saddle $\dot x=x,\ \dot y=-y$ at the origin has eigenvalues $1$ and $-1$, so it is hyperbolic.
The sink $\dot x=-x$ at the origin has the eigenvalue $-1$, so it is hyperbolic.
Non-example: the centre $\dot x=y,\ \dot y=-x$ has eigenvalues $\pm i$ with real part $0$, so it is not hyperbolic.
Non-example: $\dot x=x^2$ at $0$ has the eigenvalue $0$, so it is not hyperbolic.

reminder: A hyperbolic manifold is a connected, complete Riemannian manifold of constant sectional curvature $-1$.
definition: A hyperbolic $n$-manifold is a connected, [geodesically complete](c:geodesic-completeness) [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) of constant [sectional curvature](c:sectional-curvature) $-1$. Equivalently, it is a quotient $\mathbb{H}^n/\Gamma$ of hyperbolic space $\mathbb{H}^n$ by a discrete group $\Gamma$ of isometries that acts freely.
examples: Hyperbolic space $\mathbb{H}^n$ itself, such as the hyperbolic plane for $n=2$.
A closed surface of genus at least $2$ with a metric of curvature $-1$.
The complement of the figure-eight knot in $S^3$ has a complete hyperbolic metric of finite volume.
Non-example: the hyperbolic plane with one point removed keeps curvature $-1$ but is incomplete, so it is not a hyperbolic manifold.

steps: Take the [hyperbolic plane](c:hyperbolic-plane), the simply connected surface of constant curvature $-1$.
It is connected and complete, and it has dimension $2$.
So it is a hyperbolic manifold with $n=2$.
Higher dimensions $n$ and quotients by discrete groups give the general case.
links.why: Shows that hyperbolic manifolds extend the hyperbolic plane to all dimensions and to quotient spaces with topology.

steps: Take a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) $M$.
Ask that $M$ is connected and [geodesically complete](c:geodesic-completeness).
Ask that its sectional curvature is constantly $-1$.
A Riemannian manifold with these conditions is a hyperbolic manifold.
links.why: Shows that hyperbolic manifolds are the Riemannian manifolds with one rigid curvature condition.

reminder: A hyperbolic metric is a Riemannian metric whose curvature is $-1$ at every point.
definition: A hyperbolic metric on a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) is a metric that makes it a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) of constant [sectional curvature](c:sectional-curvature) $-1$; on a surface this is Gaussian curvature $-1$. On a Riemann surface, the hyperbolic metric means the complete conformal metric of this kind.
examples: On the open unit disc, the Poincaré metric $\frac{4|dz|^2}{(1-|z|^2)^2}$ has curvature $-1$.
On the upper half plane, $\frac{dx^2+dy^2}{y^2}$ is a hyperbolic metric.
Non-example: the flat metric $dx^2+dy^2$ on the disc has curvature $0$, and the round metric on $S^2$ has curvature $+1$, so neither is hyperbolic.

reminder: The identity of an object $X$ is the morphism $\mathrm{id}_X:X\to X$ that changes nothing when composed with any morphism.
definition: In a [category](c:category), the identity of an object $X$ is the morphism $\mathrm{id}_X:X\to X$ with $f\circ\mathrm{id}_X=f$ for every morphism $f$ out of $X$ and $\mathrm{id}_X\circ g=g$ for every morphism $g$ into $X$. For a set $X$, it is the [function](c:function) $x\mapsto x$, and [composition](c:composition) with it changes nothing.
examples: On a set $X$ the identity is the map $x\mapsto x$, and on $\mathbb{R}^n$ it corresponds to the identity matrix.
In the category of groups, the identity of $G$ is the homomorphism $g\mapsto g$.
Non-example: the map $x\mapsto-x$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is invertible but is not the identity, because composing it with $f(x)=x$ gives $-x$ and not $f$.

reminder: An implication from $A$ to $B$ says that $B$ holds whenever $A$ holds.
definition: An implication from a [proposition](c:proposition) $A$ to a proposition $B$ is a statement $A\Rightarrow B$ that is false exactly when $A$ is true and $B$ is false. Its proof-theoretic form, the entailment $A\vdash B$, says that there is a [proof](c:proof) of $B$ from the assumption $A$, and the deduction theorem links the two.
examples: The statement 'if $n$ is even, then $n^2$ is even' is a true implication.
The statement 'if $1=2$, then $3=3$' is true, because a false premise makes the implication true.
Non-example: 'if $x^2>4$, then $x>2$' does not hold for all real $x$, because $x=-3$ makes the premise true and the conclusion false.

reminder: A symbol is implicitly defined by a theory when every model fixes its meaning from the meanings of the other symbols.
definition: Let $T$ be a [first-order theory](c:first-order-theory) in a [signature](c:signature-in-logic) $\Sigma\cup\{P\}$. The symbol $P$ is implicitly defined by $T$ if any two [models](c:model) of $T$ with the same universe and the same interpretation of every symbol of $\Sigma$ also interpret $P$ in the same way. By Beth's theorem, this is equivalent to an explicit definition $T\models\forall x\,(P(x)\leftrightarrow\varphi(x))$ with $\varphi$ a formula in $\Sigma$.
examples: In the theory of groups with symbols $\cdot$ and $e$, the inverse operation is implicitly defined: the product and the unit fix every inverse.
In the theory of real closed fields with symbols $+,\cdot,0,1,\le$, the order is implicitly defined, because $x\le y$ exactly when $y-x$ is a square.
Non-example: in the theory of groups, a new unary predicate $P$ with no axioms is not implicitly defined, because $P$ can be any subset of the group.

reminder: An inequality compares two values of an ordered set with a relation such as $<$, $\le$, $>$ or $\ge$.
definition: An inequality is a statement that two expressions $x$ and $y$, with values in a [totally ordered](c:total-order) set such as the [real numbers](c:real-number), stand in the order [relation](c:relation) $x<y$, $x\le y$, $x>y$ or $x\ge y$. It is strict when it uses $<$ or $>$.
examples: $3<5$ is an inequality, and so is $x^2\ge0$ for all real $x$.
The triangle inequality $|a+b|\le|a|+|b|$.
Non-example: $x^2=4$ is an equation, not an inequality, because it states equality and not an order relation.

reminder: A bilinear form satisfies the inf-sup condition when $\inf_u\sup_v b(u,v)/(\|u\|\|v\|)$ is positive.
definition:
Let $U$ and $V$ be [Hilbert spaces](c:hilbert-space) and let $b:U	imes V	o\mathbb{R}$ be a bounded [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form). The form satisfies the inf-sup condition with constant $ eta>0$ if $\inf_{u
e0}\sup_{v
e0} rac{b(u,v)}{\|u\|\,\|v\|}\ge eta$, where the [supremum](c:least-upper-bound) is taken for each $u$. Equivalently, $\sup_{v
e0}b(u,v)/\|v\|\ge eta\|u\|$ for every $u\in U$.
examples: The inner product $b(u,v)=\langle u,v\rangle$ on a Hilbert space has $\beta=1$: take $v=u$.
Every coercive form, with $b(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2$, satisfies the condition with $\beta=\alpha$.
The Stokes divergence form $b(v,q)=-\int q\operatorname{div}v$ satisfies it between $H^1_0$ and $L^2_0$.
Non-example: $b(u,v)=\langle Tu,v\rangle$ on $\ell^2$ with $Te_n=e_n/n$ fails it, because $\sup_vb(e_n,v)/\|v\|=1/n\to0$.

steps: Take a [coercive bilinear form](c:coercive-bilinear-form) $b$ on a Hilbert space $U$ with $b(u,u)\ge\alpha\|u\|^2$.
For $u\ne0$, choose $v=u$ in the supremum.
Then $\sup_vb(u,v)/\|v\|\ge b(u,u)/\|u\|\ge\alpha\|u\|$.
So $b$ satisfies the inf-sup condition with $\beta=\alpha$.
links.why: Shows that the inf-sup condition replaces coercivity, so Lax-Milgram type results reach forms that are not coercive.

reminder: An $(\infty,n)$-category has $k$-morphisms for every $k$, and every $k$-morphism with $k>n$ is invertible.
definition: An $(\infty,n)$-category is a higher [category](c:category) with $k$-morphisms for every $k\ge0$ in which every $k$-morphism with $k>n$ is [invertible](c:isomorphism). The case $n=0$ gives an [infinity-groupoid](c:infinity-groupoid), and the case $n=1$ gives an [(infinity,1)-category](c:infinity-1-category).
examples: For $n=0$: the fundamental $\infty$-groupoid of a space.
For $n=1$: the $(\infty,1)$-category of spaces.
For $n=2$: the $(\infty,2)$-category of $(\infty,1)$-categories, with functors as morphisms and natural transformations as $2$-morphisms.
Non-example: the strict $2$-category $\mathrm{Cat}$ is an $(\infty,2)$-category but not an $(\infty,1)$-category, because its natural transformations are not all invertible.

steps: Take an [(infinity,1)-category](c:infinity-1-category) $C$.
All its $k$-morphisms with $k>1$ are invertible.
Then all its $k$-morphisms with $k>n$ are invertible, for every $n\ge1$.
So $C$ is an $(\infty,n)$-category for each $n\ge1$.
links.why: Shows that $(\infty,n)$-categories contain the usual $(\infty,1)$-categories as the case $n=1$.

steps: Take an [infinity-groupoid](c:infinity-groupoid), in which every $k$-morphism with $k\ge1$ is invertible.
Then every $k$-morphism with $k>n$ is invertible, for each $n\ge0$.
So the $\infty$-groupoid is an $(\infty,n)$-category for every $n$.
links.why: Shows that $(\infty,0)$-categories are exactly the $\infty$-groupoids, the base case of the family.

reminder: An object $I$ is injective if every morphism into $I$ from a subobject extends along the monomorphism to the whole object.
definition: An object $I$ of a [category](c:category) is injective if for every [monomorphism](c:mono) $m:A\to B$ and every morphism $f:A\to I$ there is a morphism $g:B\to I$ with $g\circ m=f$. Equivalently, $\operatorname{Hom}(-,I)$ turns monomorphisms into surjections.
examples: In the category of abelian groups, $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ are injective objects.
In the category of sets, every non-empty set is injective.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}$ is not injective among abelian groups, because the map $2\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$, $2n\mapsto n$, does not extend to $\mathbb{Z}$.

steps: Take the category of $R$-modules over a ring $R$.
Its monomorphisms are the injective module homomorphisms.
An object $E$ there is injective exactly when every map $A\to E$ extends along each injection $A\to B$.
So an injective object of this category is an [injective module](c:injective-module).
links.why: Shows that the module notion is the case of the category of modules, so general results about injective objects apply to modules.

reminder: A module $E$ is injective if every homomorphism from a submodule into $E$ extends to the whole module.
definition: A left [module](c:module) $E$ over a [ring](c:ring) $R$ is injective if for every injective homomorphism $A\to B$ of $R$-modules and every homomorphism $f:A\to E$ there is a homomorphism $B\to E$ that extends $f$. Equivalently, $\operatorname{Hom}_R(-,E)$ is an exact functor. By Baer's criterion, it is enough to test inclusions of ideals $A\subseteq R=B$.
examples: $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ are injective $\mathbb{Z}$-modules, and so is every divisible abelian group.
Every vector space over a field $k$ is an injective $k$-module.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}$ is not an injective $\mathbb{Z}$-module, because $2\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$, $2n\mapsto n$, has no extension to $\mathbb{Z}$.

steps: Take the category of $R$-modules over a ring $R$.
Its monomorphisms are the injective module homomorphisms.
An [injective object](c:injective) there has the extension property for every monomorphism $A\to B$.
So an injective module is an injective object of the category of $R$-modules.
links.why: Shows that injective modules are the injective objects of module categories, so categorical tools apply.

reminder: A measure is inner regular for finite-measure sets when it approximates each such measurable set from inside by compact subsets.
definition: A [measure](c:measure) $\mu$ on a topological space is inner regular for sets of finite measure, with respect to [compact](c:compact-space) sets, if $\mu(s)=\sup\{\mu(K) : K\subseteq s,\ K\text{ compact}\}$ for every [measurable set](c:measurable-set) $s$ with $\mu(s)<\infty$. The [supremum](c:least-upper-bound) is taken over all compact subsets $K$ of $s$.
examples: Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$ has this property.
Every Haar measure on a locally compact group has this property.
Every finite Borel measure on a Polish space has this property.
Non-example: the Dieudonné measure on the countable ordinals $[0,\omega_1)$ has total mass $1$, but every compact set is bounded and has measure $0$.

steps: Take an [inner regular](c:inner-regular) measure $\mu$: $\mu(s)=\sup\mu(K)$ over compact $K\subseteq s$ for every measurable set $s$.
Restrict this statement to the measurable sets $s$ with $\mu(s)<\infty$.
The restricted statement is exactly the condition for finite-measure sets.
So every inner regular measure satisfies this weaker condition.
links.why: Shows that this condition is a weakening of inner regularity, so theorems that need only it cover more measures.

reminder: A distribution of tangent subspaces is integrable when the Lie bracket of any two of its vector fields stays in it.
definition: A distribution $D\subseteq TM$ of $k$-dimensional subspaces of the [tangent bundle](c:tangent-bundle) is integrable, or involutive, if the [Lie bracket](c:lie-bracket) of any two [sections](c:section) of $D$ is again a section of $D$. By the Frobenius theorem, this holds exactly when through every point passes a $k$-dimensional submanifold whose tangent spaces lie in $D$.
examples: On $\mathbb{R}^n$, the distribution spanned by $\partial_1,\dots,\partial_k$ is integrable, and its leaves are the planes with $x_{k+1},\dots,x_n$ constant.
Every distribution of rank $1$ is integrable, because $[fX,gX]$ is a multiple of $X$.

Non-example: the contact distribution $\ker(dz-y\,dx)$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$, spanned by $\partial_y$ and $\partial_x+y\partial_z$, is not integrable, because the bracket of these fields is $\partial_z$, which lies outside it.

steps: Take a [distribution of subspaces](c:distribution-of-subspaces) $D$ of rank $k$ in $TM$.
Look at the Lie brackets $[X,Y]$ of sections $X,Y$ of $D$.
Require every such bracket to be a section of $D$.
A distribution with this condition is an integrable distribution.
links.why: Shows that integrability is one closure condition on a distribution, and by Frobenius it gives a foliation.
